plain: The amount you pay yourself on a covered loss before the insurance pays the rest.
The most the policy will pay for a given type of coverage.
A smaller cap inside a larger coverage, for one kind of loss (for example, water backup).
An add-on that changes a policy by adding, removing or adjusting coverage.
Something the policy generally does not cover.
Happening quickly and unexpectedly, like a hose bursting — as opposed to a slow drip over weeks.
Water that escapes slowly over a long period. These are usually treated differently from sudden leaks.
Water that comes up through a drain, sewer or sump instead of coming from a pipe. Usually needs its own add-on.
Water from rising creeks, washes or surface runoff. Usually insured separately, not under property policies.
Coverage for sudden mechanical or electrical failure of machinery such as AC or refrigeration.
Paying to replace an item with a new one, rather than its used value.
What an item was worth at the time of loss after wear is taken into account.
Extra living costs while a covered loss makes your home unlivable.
Net income and ongoing expenses covered while a covered loss temporarily closes your business.
Time at the start of a closure or outage during which the policy does not yet pay.
Perishable goods that go bad after cooling fails from a covered cause.
A power outage caused away from your building, such as a utility line failure.
Your legal responsibility when someone else is hurt or their property is damaged.
Small medical bills for injured guests paid regardless of who is at fault.
Extra repair cost to meet current building codes after a covered loss.
A building with no one living in or using it. Long vacancy can limit some coverage.
A policy expectation to keep the building heated, or to drain the water system, to prevent freeze damage.
A fire sprinkler system with water in the pipes all the time, which can freeze in unheated spaces.
The small drain pipe that carries water produced by your air conditioner outdoors. Clogs can overflow indoors.
The flexible hose connecting a fixture or appliance to the building's water pipes.
A valve that stops water flow to a fixture, a unit, or the whole building.
June 15 through September 30 in Arizona, when storms bring wind, hail, dust and flash floods.
How strongly a completed safety task is evidenced: a tap (E0), a photo (E1), a document (E2), a review (E3), or sensor data (E4).
A fix confirmed by device readings returning to normal, not just by someone saying it was done.
Your independent insurance agent, who confirms coverage decisions and can change your policy.
